solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Assertion is straightforwardly correct — students know Mumbai High is declining and that it produces associated gas. The trap is in the Reason, which correctly names a real technique (EOR at Mumbai High) but falsely extends it to 'all mature gas fields.' EOR (Enhanced Oil Recovery) is a crude oil recovery technique — water injection, polymer flooding — that has no direct application to gas field management. Students who read 'EOR' and 'Mumbai High' together accept R as true without questioning the extension to 'all mature gas fields.'
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests two independent facts: the coupled nature of associated gas production at Mumbai High, and the specificity of EOR techniques.

• Assertion (A): Correct — Mumbai High's natural gas is associated gas, produced alongside crude oil. When oil production declines due to reservoir depletion, the volume of associated gas co-produced also falls proportionally. This is an automatic, policy-independent consequence of the associated gas production mechanism.
• Reason (R): Incorrect — Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) techniques such as water injection and polymer flooding are specifically designed to improve crude oil recovery from oil reservoirs with declining natural pressure. They are NOT applicable to natural gas fields, which have different reservoir dynamics and recovery mechanisms. The claim that ONGC applies Mumbai High EOR techniques to 'all mature gas fields' is factually wrong — EOR is an oil reservoir management tool.

Correct answer: (c) A is correct but R is incorrect.

Value Addition:
• EOR methods include water flooding, gas injection, thermal methods, and chemical flooding — all targeted at oil reservoirs.
• Gas reservoir management typically uses techniques like compression, infill drilling, and pressure maintenance — not EOR.
• ONGC's Mumbai High EOR programme is one of Asia's most extensive enhanced recovery operations for a mature oil field.

solution.concept_anchor: HELP RSC vs PSC NELP — key policy shift 2016-17

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP) introduced in 2016, the Revenue Sharing Contract (RSC) model replaced Production Sharing Contracts (PSCs) for new exploration blocks.
statement_analysis.reason: HELP introduced RSCs as the standard contract form, replacing PSCs. Under RSC, the government receives a share of gross revenue from the start, eliminating cost recovery disputes.

statement_analysis.statement: Under a Revenue Sharing Contract (RSC), the government's share of revenue begins only after the contractor has fully recovered all exploration and development costs, similar to profit petroleum in a PSC.
statement_analysis.reason: This describes the PSC model (cost recovery before profit sharing), NOT the RSC model. Under RSC, the government receives its revenue share from gross revenues from the first barrel — there is no cost recovery period before government take begins.

statement_analysis.statement: ONGC operates certain exploration blocks under NELP rounds in addition to its legacy nomination blocks, meaning not all ONGC blocks were acquired under the nomination regime.
statement_analysis.reason: ONGC has participated in competitive NELP rounds and won exploration blocks in addition to its pre-NELP nomination blocks. It is incorrect to assume all ONGC blocks are nomination blocks.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three correct' is the strong distractor because Statement 2 uses real PSC terminology ('cost recovery', 'profit petroleum') that sounds like an accurate RSC description to students who haven't precisely distinguished the two contract types.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: HELP (2016) replaced PSCs with RSCs for new blocks — this is the defining feature of the policy shift. Correct.

Statement 2: The description given ('government share after full cost recovery') is precisely how a PSC works — NOT how an RSC works. Under RSC, government share starts from gross revenue immediately. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 3: ONGC has bid in NELP rounds — it holds both nomination (legacy) and NELP-awarded blocks. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct → option (a) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a sophisticated conflation trap. Students who know PSC = 'cost recovery then profit share' and RSC = 'revenue share' may not precisely recall which description goes with which contract model. Statement 2 describes a PSC mechanism but labels it as how RSC works. A partially prepared student reading 'cost recovery' and 'government share' will accept Statement 2 as describing the RSC model's obvious logic — not realising the entire premise reverses the actual RSC structure.
solution.final_explanation:
The transition from PSC to RSC is one of the most significant policy shifts in India's petroleum sector history.

• Statement 1 — Correct: HELP (2016), operationalised through OALP (2017), established RSCs as the standard contract model for all new exploration blocks. This was a deliberate policy response to the cost recovery disputes (notably KG-D6 and PMT) that plagued PSC contracts.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement describes a PSC, not an RSC. Under a PSC, contractors first recover costs from 'cost petroleum' before profit petroleum is split with the government. Under an RSC, the government receives its predetermined revenue share from gross production revenues from the very beginning — no cost recovery period exists. This structural difference is the key advantage of RSC.
• Statement 3 — Correct: ONGC has bid in NELP rounds and holds NELP-awarded exploration blocks in addition to its pre-1999 nomination blocks. The distinction matters for regulatory treatment — NELP blocks have different fiscal terms than nomination blocks.

Value Addition:
• Under RSC, operators face greater financial risk (no cost recovery guarantee) but government take is more predictable.
• The KG-D6 cost recovery dispute was a major catalyst for moving away from PSCs.
• ONGC's participation in NELP rounds demonstrates that even state companies compete under the competitive licensing framework.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Cauvery Basin trap exploits the tendency to associate it only with gas. Because gas finds in the basin received more attention, students often forget that the Cauvery Basin has both oil and gas production. Options (a) and (b) both exploit this bias — (a) says 'exclusively oil' and (b) says 'exclusively gas' — both are wrong. solution.final_explanation:
The Cauvery Basin is India's southernmost producing sedimentary basin, extending from Tamil Nadu's coastal onshore areas into the Bay of Bengal offshore.

• Option (a) — Narimanam field paired with 'Cauvery Basin, exclusively oil production': Incorrect. Narimanam is indeed a Cauvery Basin field, but it produces both oil and gas — the 'exclusively oil' qualifier makes this pairing wrong.
• Option (b) — Cauvery Basin described as 'exclusively a natural gas basin': Incorrect. This is the classic Cauvery trap. The basin produces both oil and gas — the gas association is stronger in popular memory, but oil fields also exist.
• Option (c) — Ravva field paired with 'Cauvery Basin': Incorrect. The Ravva oil and gas field is located in the Krishna-Godavari Basin (Andhra Pradesh coast), not the Cauvery Basin.
• Option (d) — Kaveri field as a Cauvery Basin field producing both oil and gas in Tamil Nadu: Correct. The Kaveri field is a Cauvery Basin asset with both oil and gas production dimensions, correctly described.

Value Addition:
• The Cauvery Basin's offshore portion holds greater unexplored potential than its producing onshore portion.
• ONGC is the primary operator in the Cauvery Basin's producing fields.
• Despite its geographic location in southern India's most populous coastal region, Cauvery Basin remains a minor national producer compared to Mumbai High or Rajasthan.
